An autodidact is a person who has taught themselves — someone whose knowledge or skills were not gained through a formal school, university, or teacher, but through their own independent effort and curiosity.

The key idea is self-directed learning. The autodidact decides what to learn, when to learn it, how to learn it, and how deeply to go. Nobody assigns them homework. Nobody grades them. Nobody tells them what to read next. They drive the entire process themselves.
What It Looks Like in Real Life

Imagine someone who never went to art school but spent years studying paintings in museums, reading books on technique, watching master artists work, and practicing obsessively on their own — until they became a skilled, respected painter. That person is an autodidact.

Or think of someone who wanted to learn computer programming. Instead of enrolling in a degree program, they bought books, watched tutorials, built projects, made mistakes, fixed them, and kept going until they could write professional-level code. Again — autodidact.

The method is always the same: self-teaching replaces (or significantly supplements) formal instruction.
A Crucial Detail: "Self-Taught" Does Not Mean "Alone"

This is where many people get confused. An autodidact is not someone who learned in total isolation, refusing all outside help. They absolutely use external resources — books, videos, libraries, the internet, conversations with experts, mentors, and so on. What makes them an autodidact is that they are the architect of their own education. They choose and assemble those resources themselves, rather than following a curriculum handed to them by an institution.

Think of the difference between a chef who graduated from culinary school (where someone else designed every lesson) versus a chef who learned by reading cookbooks, working in kitchens by observation, experimenting constantly, and seeking out specific masters to learn specific techniques. Both learned from external sources. But only the second one is an autodidact.

People become autodidacts for two broad reasons, and both are equally valid uses of the word.

By choice: Some people simply prefer self-directed learning. They find formal education too slow, too rigid, or not deep enough in the areas they care about. They trust themselves to learn better on their own terms.

By circumstance: Some people become autodidacts because formal education was not available to them — due to poverty, geography, social restriction, or historical barriers. One of the most striking historical examples is Frederick Douglass, who was enslaved in 19th-century America, where it was actually illegal to teach enslaved people to read. He secretly taught himself to read and write anyway, and went on to become one of the most powerful writers and orators of his era. He is one of history's most powerful examples of an autodidact.

Throughout history, some of the most remarkable minds were autodidacts, which tells you this is not a rare or inferior way to gain knowledge — it can produce extraordinary results.

  • Abraham Lincoln taught himself law almost entirely through independent reading. He had very little formal schooling and never attended law school, yet became a practicing lawyer and eventually the President of the United States.
  • Leonardo da Vinci had no formal training in most of the fields he mastered — anatomy, engineering, optics, geology. He learned by relentless observation, experimentation, and self-directed study.
  • Benjamin Franklin left school at age 10 and educated himself through voracious reading, becoming a scientist, inventor, writer, and statesman.
  • Jimi Hendrix never learned to read music and had no formal musical training, yet he revolutionized the electric guitar through pure self-teaching and experimentation.

It's worth clearing up a few things the word does not mean:

  • It does not mean someone who is anti-education or who looks down on schools and universities.
  • It does not mean someone who learned quickly or easily — self-teaching can be slow and hard.
  • It does not mean someone who is a genius. Autodidactism is about method, not talent or speed.
  • It does not mean someone who knows everything. An autodidact may be deeply self-taught in one or two areas while knowing very little about others.

It's also worth knowing that being an autodidact is not always an all-or-nothing label. Some people are partial autodidacts — they received some formal education in a field, but went dramatically beyond it through self-teaching. A person who studied basic music theory in school but then spent decades independently mastering jazz composition might reasonably be called an autodidact in that deeper sense.
How to Use the Word in a Sentence

• "He never went to university, but he is a true autodidact — he taught himself three languages, coding, and philosophy entirely on his own."
  • "Many of the greatest scientists in history were autodidacts who learned far more outside the classroom than inside it."
  • "As an autodidact, she designed her own reading list and worked through it with fierce discipline."

• Autodidactic (adjective) — used to describe either a person or a method of learning. "Her autodidactic approach meant she never waited for a teacher to tell her what to study next."
  • Autodidacticism (noun) — refers to the practice or philosophy of self-teaching as a concept. "Autodidacticism has produced some of humanity's greatest thinkers."
An autodidact is a self-taught person — someone who takes full ownership of their own learning, outside of or well beyond formal education, driven by their own curiosity, discipline, and initiative.
